[GDPR-4(1)] Art. 4(1) Definitions
‘personal data’ means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person (‘data subject’); an identifiable natural person is one who can be identified, directly or indirectly, in particular by reference to an identifier such as a name, an identification number, location data, an online identifier or to one or more factors specific to the physical, physiological, genetic, mental, economic, cultural or social identity of that natural person;

[GDPR-4(5)] Art. 4(5) Definitions
‘pseudonymisation’ means the processing of personal data in such a manner that the personal data can no longer be attributed to a specific data subject without the use of additional information, provided that such additional information is kept separately and is subject to technical and organisational measures to ensure that the personal data are not attributed to an identified or identifiable natural person;

[GDPR-4(13)] Art. 4(13) Definitions
‘genetic data’ means personal data relating to the inherited or acquired genetic characteristics of a natural person which give unique information about the physiology or the health of that natural person and which result, in particular, from an analysis of a biological sample from the natural person in question;

[GDPR-4(15)] Art. 4(15) Definitions
‘data concerning health’ means personal data related to the physical or mental health of a natural person, including the provision of health care services, which reveal information about his or her health status;

[GDPR-5(2)] Art. 5(2) Principles relating to processing of personal data
The controller shall be responsible for, and be able to demonstrate compliance with, paragraph 1 (‘accountability’).

[GDPR-9(1)] Art. 9(1) Processing of special categories of personal data
Processing of personal data revealing racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, or trade union membership, and the processing of genetic data, biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person, data concerning health or data concerning a natural person's sex life or sexual orientation shall be prohibited.

[GDPR-10] Art. 10 Processing of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences
Processing of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences or related security measures based on Article 6(1) shall be carried out only under the control of official authority or when the processing is authorised by Union or Member State law providing for appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of data subjects. Any comprehensive register of criminal convictions shall be kept only under the control of official authority.

[GDPR-22(1)] Art. 22(1) Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
The data subject shall have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning him or her or similarly significantly affects him or her.

[GDPR-22(4)] Art. 22(4) Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
Decisions referred to in paragraph 2 shall not be based on special categories of personal data referred to in Article 9(1), unless point (a) or (g) of Article 9(2) applies and suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's rights and freedoms and legitimate interests are in place.

[GDPR-25(1)] Art. 25(1) Data protection by design and by default
Taking into account the state of the art, the cost of implementation and the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing as well as the risks of varying likelihood and severity for rights and freedoms of natural persons posed by the processing, the controller shall, both at the time of the determination of the means for processing and at the time of the processing itself, implement appropriate technical and organisational measures, such as pseudonymisation, which are designed to implement data-protection principles, such as data minimisation, in an effective manner and to integrate the necessary safeguards into the processing in order to meet the requirements of this Regulation and protect the rights of data subjects.

[GDPR-25(2)] Art. 25(2) Data protection by design and by default
The controller shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures for ensuring that, by default, only personal data which are necessary for each specific purpose of the processing are processed. That obligation applies to the amount of personal data collected, the extent of their processing, the period of their storage and their accessibility. In particular, such measures shall ensure that by default personal data are not made accessible without the individual's intervention to an indefinite number of natural persons.

[GDPR-35(1)] Art. 35(1) Data protection impact assessment
Where a type of processing in particular using new technologies, and taking into account the nature, scope, context and purposes of the processing, is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller shall, prior to the processing, carry out an assessment of the impact of the envisaged processing operations on the protection of personal data. A single assessment may address a set of similar processing operations that present similar high risks.

[GDPR-35(3)] Art. 35(3) Data protection impact assessment
A data protection impact assessment referred to in paragraph 1 shall in particular be required in the case of:
 (a)  a systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects relating to natural persons which is based on automated processing, including profiling, and on which decisions are based that produce legal effects concerning the natural person or similarly significantly affect the natural person;
 (b)  processing on a large scale of special categories of data referred to in Article 9(1), or of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences referred to in Article 10; or
 (c)  a systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area on a large scale.

[GDPR-44] Art. 44 General principle for transfers
Any transfer of personal data which are undergoing processing or are intended for processing after transfer to a third country or to an international organisation shall take place only if, subject to the other provisions of this Regulation, the conditions laid down in this Chapter are complied with by the controller and processor, including for onward transfers of personal data from the third country or an international organisation to another third country or to another international organisation. All provisions in this Chapter shall be applied in order to ensure that the level of protection of natural persons guaranteed by this Regulation is not undermined.

[GDPR-45(1)] Art. 45(1) Transfers on the basis of an adequacy decision
A transfer of personal data to a third country or an international organisation may take place where the Commission has decided that the third country, a territory or one or more specified sectors within that third country, or the international organisation in question ensures an adequate level of protection. Such a transfer shall not require any specific authorisation.

[GDPR-46(1)] Art. 46(1) Transfers subject to appropriate safeguards
In the absence of a decision pursuant to Article 45(3), a controller or processor may transfer personal data to a third country or an international organisation only if the controller or processor has provided appropriate safeguards, and on condition that enforceable data subject rights and effective legal remedies for data subjects are available.

[GDPR-87] Art. 87 Processing of the national identification number
Member States may further determine the specific conditions for the processing of a national identification number or any other identifier of general application. In that case the national identification number or any other identifier of general application shall be used only under appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of the data subject pursuant to this Regulation.

[GDPR-R14] Recital 14
The protection afforded by this Regulation should apply to natural persons, whatever their nationality or place of residence, in relation to the processing of their personal data. This Regulation does not cover the processing of personal data which concerns legal persons and in particular undertakings established as legal persons, including the name and the form of the legal person and the contact details of the legal person.

[GDPR-R26] Recital 26
The principles of data protection should apply to any information concerning an identified or identifiable natural person. Personal data which have undergone pseudonymisation, which could be attributed to a natural person by the use of additional information should be considered to be information on an identifiable natural person. To determine whether a natural person is identifiable, account should be taken of all the means reasonably likely to be used, such as singling out, either by the controller or by another person to identify the natural person directly or indirectly. To ascertain whether means are reasonably likely to be used to identify the natural person, account should be taken of all objective factors, such as the costs of and the amount of time required for identification, taking into consideration the available technology at the time of the processing and technological developments. The principles of data protection should therefore not apply to anonymous information, namely information which does not relate to an identified or identifiable natural person or to personal data rendered anonymous in such a manner that the data subject is not or no longer identifiable. This Regulation does not therefore concern the processing of such anonymous information, including for statistical or research purposes.

[GDPR-R35] Recital 35
Personal data concerning health should include all data pertaining to the health status of a data subject which reveal information relating to the past, current or future physical or mental health status of the data subject. This includes information about the natural person collected in the course of the registration for, or the provision of, health care services as referred to in Directive 2011/24/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council (9) to that natural person; a number, symbol or particular assigned to a natural person to uniquely identify the natural person for health purposes; information derived from the testing or examination of a body part or bodily substance, including from genetic data and biological samples; and any information on, for example, a disease, disability, disease risk, medical history, clinical treatment or the physiological or biomedical state of the data subject independent of its source, for example from a physician or other health professional, a hospital, a medical device or an in vitro diagnostic test.

[AIA-Art12(1)] Art. 12(1) Record-keeping
High-risk AI systems shall technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system.

[AIA-Art12(2)] Art. 12(2) Record-keeping
In order to ensure a level of traceability of the functioning of a high-risk AI system that is appropriate to the intended purpose of the system, logging capabilities shall enable the recording of events relevant for:
 (a)  identifying situations that may result in the high-risk AI system presenting a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) or in a substantial modification;
 (b)  facilitating the post-market monitoring referred to in Article 72; and
 (c)  monitoring the operation of high-risk AI systems referred to in Article 26(5).

[AIA-Art19(1)] Art. 19(1) Automatically generated logs
Providers of high-risk AI systems shall keep the logs referred to in Article 12(1), automatically generated by their high-risk AI systems, to the extent such logs are under their control. Without prejudice to applicable Union or national law, the logs shall be kept for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months, unless provided otherwise in the applicable Union or national law, in particular in Union law on the protection of personal data.

[AIA-Art26(6)] Art. 26(6) Obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems
Deployers of high-risk AI systems shall keep the logs automatically generated by that high-risk AI system to the extent such logs are under their control, for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months, unless provided otherwise in applicable Union or national law, in particular in Union law on the protection of personal data.
 Deployers that are financial institutions subject to requirements regarding their internal governance, arrangements or processes under Union financial services law shall maintain the logs as part of the documentation kept pursuant to the relevant Union financial service law.

[AIA-Art26(11)] Art. 26(11) Obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems
Without prejudice to Article 50 of this Regulation, deployers of high-risk AI systems referred to in Annex III that make decisions or assist in making decisions related to natural persons shall inform the natural persons that they are subject to the use of the high-risk AI system. For high-risk AI systems used for law enforcement purposes Article 13 of Directive (EU) 2016/680 shall apply.

[AIA-Art50(1)] Art. 50(1) Transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems
Providers shall ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed in such a way that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect, taking into account the circumstances and the context of use. This obligation shall not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties, unless those systems are available for the public to report a criminal offence.

[AIA-Art86(1)] Art. 86(1) Right to explanation of individual decision-making
Any affected person subject to a decision which is taken by the deployer on the basis of the output from a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III, with the exception of systems listed under point 2 thereof, and which produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects that person in a way that they consider to have an adverse impact on their health, safety or fundamental rights shall have the right to obtain from the deployer clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken.

[POL-1.1] Definitions
Insured person: the person named on the policy schedule. Claim: a request for reimbursement or payment under this policy. Claims handler: the insurer's employee authorised to decide claims. Medical adviser: the physician who advises the insurer on medical questions under professional secrecy.

[POL-2.1] Own risk
The insured pays the first EUR 385 of covered medical costs in each calendar year (own risk). GP consultations, maternity care and costs for children under 18 do not count toward the own risk.

[POL-2.2] Physiotherapy
Physiotherapy is covered up to 9 sessions per calendar year under the supplementary package, on referral by a GP or specialist. Sessions after surgery on the knee, hip or spine are covered without referral for the first 12 weeks after the operation.

[POL-2.3] Hospital care
Hospital admission, surgery and emergency care are covered in full after the own risk, at contracted hospitals. At non-contracted hospitals reimbursement is limited to 75 percent of the market rate, except in an emergency.

[POL-2.4] Mental health care
Treatment by a registered psychologist or psychiatrist is covered after the own risk on referral by a GP, for diagnosed conditions. Coaching and preventive sessions are not covered.

[POL-2.5] Medical aids
Hearing aids are covered at 75 percent of the purchase price up to EUR 1,500 per aid every five years, on prescription by an ENT specialist or audiologist. Insulin pens and glucose test strips are covered in full on prescription.

[POL-2.6] Maternity care
Antenatal checks, two routine ultrasounds (around 12 and 20 weeks) and delivery care by a midwife are covered in full and do not count toward the own risk.

[POL-3.1] Travel: medical costs abroad
Emergency medical costs abroad, including hospital admission, are covered up to the cost of the same care at home, and in full inside the EU with a valid EHIC. The insured must notify the emergency line within 48 hours of an admission.

[POL-3.2] Travel: luggage
Lost, stolen or damaged luggage is covered up to EUR 1,500 per trip, with a limit of EUR 500 per item. Theft must be reported to the police within 24 hours; loss by an airline requires the airline's property irregularity report. Receipts or proof of value are required.

[POL-4.1] Claim documents
A claim must include the claim form, an itemised invoice, and for medical costs the referral or prescription where this policy requires one. The insurer may request further documents; medical documents are requested by and sent to the medical adviser only.

[POL-4.2] Claim deadlines
Claims must be submitted within 12 months of the treatment or incident. The insurer decides within 30 days of receiving a complete claim and informs the insured of the reasons for any reduction or rejection.

[POL-4.3] Exclusions
Not covered: cosmetic treatment without medical necessity, costs caused by intent or by driving under the influence, and care received before the policy start date for a condition known to the insured.

[POL-5.1] How claims are decided
Every decision on a claim outcome, to pay, reduce or reject, is taken by a claims handler, who decides. Automated tools may check completeness, extract amounts and prepare a recommendation; they do not decide the claim. The insured may ask for the reasons and contest a decision.

[POL-5.2] Health data in claims
Health data in a claim is processed only as far as needed to assess that claim, only by staff bound to secrecy, and medical judgement is given by the medical adviser. Health data from one policy is not used for another policy without explicit consent.

[MED-1] Medical necessity: general test
A treatment is medically necessary when it is appropriate for the diagnosed condition, in line with accepted medical practice, not mainly for convenience, and the least costly option that is equally effective. Whether a specific treatment meets this test is decided by the medical adviser, not by the claims assistant or the claims handler. Synthetic insurer guideline for the demo, not medical advice.

[MED-2] Documents that support a medical claim
A medical claim is complete when it has an itemised invoice from a registered provider (date, service code or description, amount), the referral or prescription where the policy requires one, and for hospital or emergency care a discharge note or medical report. Missing items are requested from the claimant; medical reports are sent to the medical adviser only. Synthetic insurer guideline.

[MED-3] Physiotherapy
Physiotherapy is reimbursed per session up to the policy limit (see POL-2.2). After an operation on the knee, hip or spine, sessions in the first 12 weeks need no referral. More sessions than the limit, or sessions without a clear link to an injury or operation, go to the medical adviser for a necessity opinion. Synthetic insurer guideline.

[MED-4] Emergency care abroad
Emergency care abroad is care that cannot wait until the insured returns home: an accident, a fracture, acute illness or hospital admission. It is covered under the travel cover (see POL-3.1). The insured must notify the emergency line within 48 hours of an admission. Ambulance transport to the nearest suitable hospital is part of emergency care. Repatriation needs the medical adviser's approval. Synthetic insurer guideline.

[MED-5] Causality between an incident and a treatment
For accident and travel claims, the treatment must follow from the reported incident: the dates must be consistent and the treatment must fit the injury described. A gap of more than 14 days between incident and first treatment, or a treatment that does not fit the reported injury, is referred to the medical adviser. The claims assistant flags the inconsistency; it does not judge the medicine. Synthetic insurer guideline.

[MED-6] Mental health claims
Treatment by a registered psychologist or psychiatrist is covered on GP referral for a diagnosed condition (see POL-2.4). The claims assistant checks only that a referral and an itemised invoice are present. The diagnosis, the treatment plan and the number of sessions needed are for the medical adviser. Mental health details never leave the insurer's perimeter. Synthetic insurer guideline.

[MED-7] Medical aids
Hearing aids, mobility aids and similar devices are reimbursed on prescription from the relevant specialist, at the percentage and limits in the policy (see POL-2.5). A rental for a temporary need, such as a wheelchair while a fracture heals, is reimbursed for the prescribed period. Synthetic insurer guideline.

[MED-8] Reasonable and customary charges
An invoice is checked against the usual charge for the same service in the same region. A charge far above the usual level is not refused by the assistant; it is flagged for the claims handler, who may pay up to the usual level and ask the provider for an explanation. Synthetic insurer guideline.

[MED-9] When the claims handler must be involved
Every outcome (pay in full, pay in part, reject, ask for documents) is the claims handler's decision. The assistant prepares a recommendation with the policy clauses and criteria it rests on and the questions it could not answer. Suspected fraud, disputed policy wording and exclusions go to the legal reviewer. Synthetic insurer guideline.

[MED-10] Lost or damaged luggage
A luggage claim needs proof of value (receipts, bank statements or photos), and for loss by an airline the property irregularity report; for theft, a police report within 24 hours. Payment is limited per item and per trip (see POL-3.2). Items above the per-item limit are paid up to the limit. Synthetic insurer guideline.

[CJEU-C-634/21] SCHUFA Holding (Scoring), 7 December 2023
Operative part: Article 22(1) GDPR 'must be interpreted as meaning that the automated establishment, by a credit information agency, of a probability value based on personal data relating to a person and concerning his or her ability to meet payment commitments in the future constitutes "automated individual decision-making" within the meaning of that provision, where a third party, to which that probability value is transmitted, draws strongly on that probability value to establish, implement or terminate a contractual relationship with that person.' Para. 52: Article 22(1) 'lays down a prohibition in principle'. Consequence for claims: a recommendation must remain advice that a claims handler weighs and can depart from; if handlers in practice draw strongly on it, the recommendation itself risks being the decision.

[CJEU-C-413/23P] EDPS v SRB, 4 September 2025
Judgment on Regulation 2018/1725 (EU institutions), whose definitions match the GDPR. Operative part: sets aside the General Court's judgment in T-557/20 and refers the case back. Para. 86: pseudonymised data 'must not be regarded as constituting, in all cases and for every person, personal data', in so far as pseudonymisation may 'effectively prevent persons other than the controller from identifying the data subject'. Para. 77: that presupposes that the recipient cannot lift the measures and that the measures prevent attribution 'including by recourse to other means of identification such as cross-checking with other factors'. Paras. 111 and 112: for the duty to inform about recipients, identifiability is assessed 'at the time of collection of the data and from the point of view of the controller', irrespective of whether the data are personal for the recipient. Consequence: placeholders lower the risk of a cloud transfer, but the insurer still treats the data as personal, names the recipients in its privacy notice and records the transfer.

[CJEU-C-184/20] OT v Vyriausioji tarnybinės etikos komisija, 1 August 2022
Operative part, point 2: Article 9(1) GDPR covers the publication of 'personal data that are liable to disclose indirectly the sexual orientation of a natural person'. Para. 127: the special-category regime is not excluded for 'personal data that are liable indirectly to reveal sensitive information'. Para. 120 frames the test as data revealing a special category 'by means of an intellectual operation involving comparison or deduction'. Consequence: an invoice line, medication or hospital name from which a health condition can be deduced is health data.

[CJEU-C-236/09] Test-Achats, 1 March 2011
Operative part: 'Article 5(2) of Council Directive 2004/113/EC ... is invalid with effect from 21 December 2012.' That provision let Member States keep sex-based differences in insurance premiums and benefits; para. 32 finds it 'incompatible with Articles 21 and 23 of the Charter'. The case is about sex, not ethnicity; for ethnic origin the controlling rule is Directive 2000/43/EC, Art. 2 and Art. 3(1)(h) (access to goods and services). Consequence: insurance premiums and benefits may not differ by sex, and selecting claims by ethnic origin or a proxy for it is discrimination.

[CJEU-C-582/14] Breyer, 19 October 2016
Operative part, point 1: a dynamic IP address is personal data for a website operator 'where the latter has the legal means which enable it to identify the data subject with additional data which the internet service provider has about that person'. Para. 46: a means is not reasonably likely to be used where identification is 'prohibited by law or practically impossible', so that 'the risk of identification appears in reality to be insignificant'. Consequence: identifiability counts the means a party can lawfully obtain through someone else, so a recipient that can link a placeholder back through another party still holds personal data.

[EDPB-01/2025] EDPB Guidelines 01/2025 on pseudonymisation (adopted 16 January 2025, version for public consultation)
Executive summary: 'Pseudonymised data, which could be attributed to a natural person by the use of additional information, is to be considered information on an identifiable natural person, and is therefore personal. This statement also holds true if pseudonymised data and additional information are not in the hands of the same person.' Pseudonymisation may 'help guarantee an essentially equivalent level of protection for data they intend to export', but 'pseudonymisation alone will normally not be a sufficient measure'. The controller defines a pseudonymisation domain and keeps the additional information (the key) outside it.

[WP251] Guidelines on automated decision-making and profiling (WP251rev.01)
Page 21: 'The controller cannot avoid the Article 22 provisions by fabricating human involvement.' Human oversight must be 'meaningful, rather than just a token gesture. It should be carried out by someone who has the authority and competence to change the decision. As part of the analysis, they should consider all the relevant data.' Page 23: a controller relying on the contract exception in Art. 22(2)(a) 'must be able to show that this type of processing is necessary, taking into account whether a less privacy-intrusive method could be adopted.'

[EIOPA-AI-2025] EIOPA Opinion on AI governance and risk management, EIOPA-BoS-25-360, 6 August 2025
Para. 2.4: the AI Act identifies as high-risk 'the use of AI systems for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in the case of life and health insurance'. Paras. 2.5 and 2.6: the Opinion covers insurance AI systems that are not prohibited or high-risk; para. 2.1 names claims management as one such use. Para. 3.7: undertakings should develop risk-based and proportionate governance covering fairness and ethics, data governance, documentation and record keeping, transparency and explainability, human oversight, and accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity. Para. 3.28: customers should be informed that they are interacting with an AI system and, on request, told the influence of the AI system on a decision with a material impact on them.

[OWASP-LLM01] OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications: LLM01 Prompt Injection
Summary: instructions embedded in user input or documents can alter an LLM's behaviour. Mitigations include constraining model behaviour, segregating untrusted content, requiring human approval for privileged actions, and enforcing decisions outside the model.

[UAVG-30(3)(b)] NL UAVG Art. 30(3)(b) Health data: insurers (version in force from 1 September 2026)
'Gelet op artikel 9, tweede lid, onderdeel g en h, van de verordening, is het verbod om gegevens over gezondheid te verwerken niet van toepassing indien de verwerking geschiedt door: ... b. verzekeraars als bedoeld in artikel 1:1 van de Wet op het financieel toezicht ..., voor zover de verwerking noodzakelijk is voor: 1°. de beoordeling van het door de verzekeraar te verzekeren risico en de betrokkene geen bezwaar heeft gemaakt; of 2°. de uitvoering van de overeenkomst van verzekering dan wel het assisteren bij het beheer en de uitvoering van de verzekering.' Our translation: on the basis of GDPR Art. 9(2)(g) and (h), the ban on processing health data does not apply to insurers as far as necessary to assess the risk to be insured (if the data subject has not objected) or to perform the insurance contract.

[UAVG-30(4)] NL UAVG Art. 30(4) Secrecy for health data
'Indien toepassing wordt gegeven aan het eerste, tweede of derde lid, worden de gegevens alleen verwerkt door personen die uit hoofde van ambt, beroep of wettelijk voorschrift dan wel krachtens een overeenkomst tot geheimhouding zijn verplicht.' Our translation: where paragraphs 1 to 3 apply, the data are processed only by persons bound to secrecy by office, profession, statutory rule or a confidentiality agreement.

[UAVG-40] NL UAVG Art. 40 Exceptions to the ban on automated decisions
'Artikel 22, eerste lid, van de verordening geldt niet indien de in die bepaling bedoelde geautomatiseerde individuele besluitvorming, anders dan op basis van profilering, noodzakelijk is om te voldoen aan een wettelijke verplichting die op de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke rust of noodzakelijk is voor de vervulling van een taak van algemeen belang.' Our translation: Art. 22(1) does not apply where automated decision-making, other than on the basis of profiling, is necessary to comply with a legal obligation of the controller or to perform a task in the public interest. A private insurer's claims decision is neither, so this Art. 22(2)(b) law does not cover it.

[UAVG-46] NL UAVG Art. 46 National identification number
'Een nummer dat ter identificatie van een persoon bij wet is voorgeschreven, wordt bij de verwerking van persoonsgegevens slechts gebruikt ter uitvoering van de desbetreffende wet dan wel voor doeleinden bij de wet bepaald.' Our translation: a number prescribed by law to identify a person (such as the BSN) is used only to carry out that law or for purposes set by law. This is the Dutch use of GDPR Art. 87.

[ZVW-86] NL Zorgverzekeringswet Art. 86 BSN in health insurance (version in force from 1 January 2026)
Art. 86(1): 'neemt de zorgverzekeraar met het oog op de uitvoering van de zorgverzekering en van deze wet het burgerservicenummer van zijn verzekerde ... in zijn administratie op.' Art. 86(3): 'De zorgverzekeraar gebruikt het burgerservicenummer van de verzekerde met het doel te waarborgen dat de in het kader van de verzekering van zorg te verwerken persoonsgegevens op die verzekerde betrekking hebben.' Our translation: the health insurer records the insured's BSN and uses it to make sure that personal data processed for the insurance relate to that insured person. Art. 13 of the Wet aanvullende bepalingen verwerking persoonsgegevens in de zorg (BWBR0023864) applies the same rule to supplementary health insurers.

[ZVW-87] NL Zorgverzekeringswet Art. 87(1) and (5) Health data from care providers; secrecy
Art. 87(1): a care provider that bills the insurer directly gives it the insured's personal data, 'waaronder gegevens over gezondheid ..., die noodzakelijk zijn voor de uitvoering van de zorgverzekering'. Art. 87(5): staff of the health insurer not already bound by professional secrecy 'zijn verplicht tot geheimhouding van de gegevens'. Our translation: care providers send the health data needed to perform the insurance, and insurer staff are bound to secrecy about them.

[GVPV-5.1.1] Gedragscode Verwerking Persoonsgegevens Verzekeraars 2024, art. 5.1.1
'De Verzekeraar verwerkt alleen Gezondheidsgegevens als: (a) de Betrokkene uitdrukkelijke toestemming heeft verleend; of (b) dit noodzakelijk is voor de beoordeling en acceptatie van een Betrokkene en het uitvoeren van een verzekering. ... De Verzekeraar mag Gezondheidsgegevens die de Betrokkene aan de medisch adviseur heeft verstrekt in verband met een verzekering niet gebruiken voor een andere verzekering, tenzij de Betrokkene hiervoor uitdrukkelijke toestemming verleent' (points (c) to (h) list further grounds). Our translation: the insurer processes health data only with explicit consent or where necessary to assess, accept and perform an insurance; health data given to the medical adviser for one insurance is not used for another without explicit consent.

[GVPV-5.1.3] Gedragscode Verwerking Persoonsgegevens Verzekeraars 2024, art. 5.1.3
'Alleen de Medisch Adviseur mag Gezondheidsgegevens verwerken voor het opstellen van een medisch advies.' The medical adviser is not responsible for health data processed by 'de (i) Technisch Acceptant en claimbehandelaar; (ii) personen binnen de Verzekeraar die rechtstreeks van de Betrokkene Gezondheidsgegevens hebben verkregen, al dan niet gelijktijdig met het melden van een claim of schade, als deze Gezondheidsgegevens noodzakelijk zijn voor verdere beoordeling daarvan'. The explanatory notes separate the medical adviser's advice from the claims handler's decision. Our translation: only the medical adviser may process health data to write a medical opinion; claims handlers may process health data received with a claim when needed to assess it.

[GVPV-4.2.2] Gedragscode Verwerking Persoonsgegevens Verzekeraars 2024, art. 4.2.2 Automated decisions
Insurers may take fully automated decisions on entering into or performing an insurance only if the decision '(a) noodzakelijk is voor het aangaan of uitvoeren van de verzekering; of (b) berust op uitdrukkelijke toestemming van de Betrokkene; of (c) uitvoering geeft aan een publiekrechtelijke taak of wettelijke verplichting', with the right to give one's view, contest the decision and have a human reconsider it, and a DPIA beforehand. Our translation and note: the Dutch code accepts the Art. 22(2)(a) contract exception for insurance decisions; keeping a human decision-maker is our choice, not a legal minimum.

[AP-DPIA-7] Dutch DPA list of processing that needs a DPIA (Staatscourant 2019, 64418), item 7
'Gezondheidsgegevens. Grootschalige verwerkingen van gegevens over gezondheid (bijvoorbeeld door instellingen of voorzieningen voor gezondheidszorg ..., verzekeraars, en onderzoeksinstituten)'. Our translation: large-scale processing of health data, for example by insurers, requires a DPIA (GDPR Art. 35(4)).

[BDSG-22] DE BDSG § 22(1) and (2) Special categories
§ 22(1) no. 1(b) allows special-category processing for health care, treatment or the management of health systems 'oder aufgrund eines Vertrags der betroffenen Person mit einem Angehörigen eines Gesundheitsberufs', by medical staff or others bound to secrecy. § 22(2) lists safeguards, including pseudonymisation, encryption, logging of who entered or changed data, and restricted access. Note: § 22 has no insurer ground; German insurers rely on consent (Art. 9(2)(a) with VVG § 213) and on Art. 9(2)(f).

[BDSG-37] DE BDSG § 37 Automated decisions in insurance
§ 37(1): beyond Art. 22(2)(a) and (c), the right not to be subject to an automated decision does not apply where the decision is made in providing benefits under an insurance contract and '1. dem Begehren der betroffenen Person stattgegeben wurde oder 2. die Entscheidung auf der Anwendung verbindlicher Entgeltregelungen für Heilbehandlungen beruht', with the right to human intervention, to state one's view and to contest. § 37(2): such decisions may be based on health data. Our translation: Germany allows automated claims decisions that grant the claim in full, or that apply binding medical fee schedules.

[VVG-213] DE VVG § 213 Collecting health data from third parties
§ 213(1): an insurer may collect health data only from doctors, hospitals, care homes, other personal insurers, statutory health funds and authorities, and only 'soweit die Kenntnis der Daten für die Beurteilung des zu versichernden Risikos oder der Leistungspflicht erforderlich ist und die betroffene Person eine Einwilligung erteilt hat.' Our translation: only where needed to assess the risk or the duty to pay, and with the data subject's consent; the person is informed beforehand and may object (§ 213(2)).

[RED-2000/43-2] Racial Equality Directive 2000/43/EC, Art. 2 and Art. 3(1)(h)
Art. 2(1): 'the principle of equal treatment shall mean that there shall be no direct or indirect discrimination based on racial or ethnic origin.' Art. 2(2)(b): indirect discrimination occurs 'where an apparently neutral provision, criterion or practice would put persons of a racial or ethnic origin at a particular disadvantage'. Art. 3(1)(h): the Directive applies to 'access to and supply of goods and services which are available to the public'. Consequence: selecting claims by surname or country of birth is at least indirect discrimination on ethnic origin.

[UAVG-31] NL UAVG Art. 31 Criminal offence data: only under the listed exceptions
'Onverminderd artikel 10 van de verordening mogen persoonsgegevens van strafrechtelijke aard alleen worden verwerkt voor zover dit krachtens de artikelen 32 en 33 is toegestaan.' Our translation: without prejudice to GDPR Art. 10, personal data on criminal convictions and offences may be processed only as far as Articles 32 and 33 allow.

[UAVG-33(2)] NL UAVG Art. 33(2) Criminal offence data: a controller's own purposes
'Persoonsgegevens van strafrechtelijke aard mogen worden verwerkt door de verwerkingsverantwoordelijke die deze gegevens ten eigen behoeve verwerkt: a. ter beoordeling van een verzoek van betrokkene om een beslissing over hem te nemen of aan hem een prestatie te leveren; of b. ter bescherming van zijn belangen, voor zover het gaat om strafbare feiten die zijn of op grond van feiten en omstandigheden naar verwachting zullen worden gepleegd jegens hem of jegens personen die in zijn dienst zijn.' Our translation: a controller may process criminal offence data for its own purposes (a) to assess a request by the data subject for a decision about them or a performance for them, such as an insurance claim, or (b) to protect its interests against offences committed or expected against it or its staff.

[CHARTER-21] Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, Art. 21 Non-discrimination
Art. 21(1): 'Any discrimination based on any ground such as sex, race, colour, ethnic or social origin, genetic features, language, religion or belief, political or any other opinion, membership of a national minority, property, birth, disability, age or sexual orientation shall be prohibited.' Art. 21(2): 'Within the scope of application of the Treaties and without prejudice to any of their specific provisions, any discrimination on grounds of nationality shall be prohibited.'

[AIA-Art113] EU AI Act Art. 113, third paragraph, point (c), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 Art. 1(40): when the high-risk duties apply
'(c) Chapter III, Sections 1, 2, and 3, with the exception of Article 6(5), shall apply from: (i) 2 December 2027 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III; and (ii) 2 August 2028 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(1) and Annex I'. Consequence: the high-risk duties on logs, human oversight and deployers (Arts. 12, 14, 19, 26) bind Annex III systems from 2 December 2027.

[METHOD-PRIVACY-TRIAGE] Privacy use-case triage (claude-for-legal, privacy-legal)
Before an assessment, classify a processing activity as PROCEED (no assessment, standard safeguards), PIA REQUIRED (assessment before or alongside deployment), DPIA MANDATORY (a regime trigger is met; under GDPR see Art. 35), or STOP (conflicts with the privacy policy or has no lawful basis as described; redesign first). Steps: understand the activity; check house triggers; check mandatory assessment triggers for every regime in scope, citing the controlling provision with a pinpoint; check the activity against every privacy-policy commitment (collection, sharing, retention, purpose, rights). Strong indicators that warrant an assessment even without a mandatory trigger: new technology, children's data, combining datasets collected separately, data that could enable discrimination, processing users would not expect. A direct policy conflict means STOP, not 'proceed with caution'. For claims: an AI assistant that processes health data in claims is new technology plus special-category data, so a DPIA under GDPR Art. 35 is the conservative reading.

[METHOD-PIA] Privacy impact assessment structure (claude-for-legal, privacy-legal)
A PIA or DPIA covers, in order: an executive summary; a description of the processing (what, why, which data, which systems); the lawful basis, regime by regime; the data flow (collection, storage, access, transfers, retention, deletion); consistency with the privacy policy; risks and mitigations, each risk specific to this processing with likelihood, severity and the control that addresses it; data subject rights (access, rectification, erasure, objection, the right not to be subject to automated decisions); and a recommendation. A DPIA submitted to a regulator (prior consultation, GDPR Art. 36) is gated on legal sign-off.

[METHOD-AI-TRIAGE] AI use-case triage (claude-for-legal, ai-governance-legal)
Classify an AI use case as APPROVED, CONDITIONAL (approved with required controls, or pending an AI impact assessment), or NOT APPROVED. Ask what the AI does (generates, decides, recommends, automates), who it acts on (employees, customers, third parties), whether a human reviews the output before anything happens, which vendor, and whether it touches external parties. A use case not in the registry defaults to CONDITIONAL pending an impact assessment. Red lines are an automatic no and are not softened. Check every jurisdiction where affected people are, not only where the company sits; a use case that crosses jurisdictions gets the strictest applicable treatment. For claims: the assistant recommends and a claims handler decides, so the use case is CONDITIONAL with controls (human review, logging, data minimisation), and a final automated decision on a claim is a red line.

[METHOD-AIA] AI impact assessment and vendor AI review (claude-for-legal, ai-governance-legal)
An AI impact assessment records the system's purpose, the people affected, the data used, the human oversight in place, foreseeable harms (accuracy, bias, privacy, security, transparency) with mitigations, the applicable regulatory obligations per jurisdiction, and the residual risk with a named owner. For a vendor AI tool: what data the vendor receives, whether it trains on customer data, where it processes and stores data, sub-processors, retention, security certifications, contractual commitments (data processing agreement, transfer mechanism), and the right to audit. For claims: the cloud models behind BRANE are vendor AI; the assessment records that only placeholdered or health-free payloads reach them and which transfer mechanism covers the provider.

[METHOD-CITATIONS] Source attribution and verification tiers (claude-for-legal)
Every regulatory citation carries a tag. Settled: stable, well-known references unlikely to have changed. Verify: real but should be checked (delegated acts, regulator guidance, standards, effective dates, thresholds, recent amendments). Verify-pinpoint: article numbers, annex references, subsection letters and paragraph numbers carry the highest fabrication risk and must always be checked against the primary source; EU AI Act article numbers shifted during consolidation, so every pinpoint to the Act is checked against the Official Journal text. Retrieved citations name their source (EUR-Lex, regulator site). For non-lawyer users, uncertain dates and thresholds go in a list to confirm with counsel rather than inline. Every output is a draft for review by a qualified person, not legal advice.

[METHOD-TRANSFERS] International transfers watch (claude-for-legal, privacy-legal currency watch)
For transfers of personal data outside the EEA: the EU-US Data Privacy Framework has applied since July 2023 and is subject to litigation, so verify it is still valid before relying on it; for other destinations check the Commission's current adequacy list; otherwise use standard contractual clauses with a transfer impact assessment (GDPR Art. 46). Verify every date and status against a current source; a stale watch list is worse than none.
